units.title: Introduction to Organic Chemistry
units.intro: Organic chemistry = chemistry of carbon compounds (plus H, and often O, N, X…). Carbon has 4 valence electrons → four bonds, long chains, rings, single / double / triple bonds.

cards.title: Organic vs inorganic
body: Organic: covalent, often low m.p., burn to CO₂ + H₂O, may show isomerism. Inorganic: often ionic, high m.p., no typical combustion to CO₂.

cards.title: 2.1.1 Introduction
body: Until the early 19th century, chemists had managed to make many simple compounds in the laboratory, but were still unable to produce the complex molecules that they found in living organisms.
From this, the idea that there was a “vital force” in the formation of organic compounds was developed.
One consequence of this vital force, chemists believed, was that organic compounds could not be prepared and manipulated in the laboratory as inorganic compounds could.
In 1928, Friedrich Wohler discovered that it was possible to convert the inorganic salt ammonium cyanate into the organic substance urea, which had previously been found in human urine.

cards.title: 2.1.2 Some Differences between Organic and Inorganic Compounds
body: Although organic compounds are governed by the same laws that apply to inorganic compounds, their properties can sometimes be quite different from those of inorganic compounds.
The number of known organic compounds is in the millions, while that of inorganic compounds is in the hundreds of thousands.
All organic compounds are made of carbon.
Carbon is a unique non-metal found in group IV of the Periodic Table.

cards.title: 2.1.3 Classification of Organic Compounds
body: In a very broad sense organic compounds can be divided into two groups: those that have an open-chain structure and those that are cyclic or their structures include rings.
Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with organic molecules.
Plants use sunlight to convert carbon dioxide in the air into organic compounds through the process of photosynthesis.
Animals and other organisms then feed on plants to obtain their own organic compounds.

body: Open chain (aliphatic) vs cyclic. Saturated (only single C–C) vs unsaturated (double / triple). Aromatic = contains a benzene ring.

Alkyl group = alkane minus one H: methyl −CH₃, ethyl −C₂H₅.

cards.title: IUPAC for branched alkanes (phone checklist)
body:
1. Longest continuous chain = parent.
2. Number from the end nearest a branch.
3. Name branches as alkyl groups with locants (2-methyl…).
4. If two identical branches: di-, tri-; list different branches alphabetically.
5. Cyclo- in front for rings (cyclopropane, cyclohexane).

cards.title: Alkenes & alkynes
body: Number the chain so the multiple bond gets the lowest number. Ethene C₂H₄, propene C₃H₆, ethyne C₂H₂.
**Saturated** = full of hydrogens (alkanes). **Unsaturated** = can add more atoms across the multiple bond.

cards.title: Reaction switch
body: Alkanes: substitute (need UV for halogenation). Alkenes/alkynes: add (H₂, Br₂, HCl, H₂O). Decolourising bromine water is the classroom test for C=C.

cards.title: Benzene / aromatics
body: Six-carbon ring with delocalised electrons. Does not behave like a normal alkene — prefers substitution so the ring stays intact.

cards.title: Petroleum
body: Mixture of hydrocarbons. Separated by **fractional distillation** (different boiling points). Heavier fractions can be **cracked** into smaller, more useful alkenes and petrol-range alkanes.

cards.title: 2.2.1 Introduction
body: Almost all organic compounds are considered as derivatives of hydrocarbons.
Chemical Bonding and Formulas of Hydrocarbons A carbon atom is tetravalent or always forms four bonds.
In organic chemistry, organic molecules are, most of the time, represented by using molecular formula, structural formula or condensed structural formula.

cards.title: 2.2.2 The Alkanes Series
body: The alkane series comprises the simplest aliphatic hydrocarbons.
The general formula of the alkane series is CnH2n+2, where n = 1, 2, 3, etc.
All side branches are called substituent groups, because they appear as a substitute for a hydrogen atom in the straight chain.

cards.title: 2.2.3 The Alkenes Series
body: A basic principle of the IUPAC system is that the functional groups are to be given a preferred status in the naming of a compound.
The different types of isomerism shown by alkenes are: skeletal or chain isomerism, position isomerism, and geometric or cis-trans isomerism.
A set of alkenes with the same formula may have the same number of carbon atoms in their skeleton, but the location of either the double bond or the substituents attached to the skeleton may differ.

cards.title: 2.2.4 The Alkynes Series
body: Many of the alkynes are used to synthesize other chemical products.
The raw materials that are needed to make acetylene are calcium carbonate and coal.
An important use of acetylene is in oxyacetylene gas welding.

cards.title: 2.2.5 Aromatic Compounds
body: The term “aromatic” was originally used because many of the benzene-related compounds known in the 19th century were found in pleasant-smelling (aroma) oils that came from spices, fruits and other plant parts.
Benzene itself and other organic compounds that contain benzene rings as part of their structure are called aromatic compounds, whether they have odour or not.
In 1865 the German chemist, Friedrick August Kekule, proposed a different kind of structure for benzene: a hexagon of carbon atoms with alternating single and double bonds.

**Step 2: Contrast physical behaviors**

**Step 3: Final Result**
Organic compounds are characterized by **predominantly covalent bonding**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the systematic IUPAC name for the branched alkane with the formula $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$$?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Find the longest continuous carbon chain**
The chain has four carbon atoms, so the parent name is **butane**.

**Step 2: Number the parent chain**
Number from left to right to give the methyl substituent the lowest possible number:
$$\text{C}_1(\text{CH}_3)-\text{C}_2\text{H(CH}_3)-\text{C}_3\text{H}_2-\text{C}_4\text{H}_3$$
This places the methyl branch at carbon-2. Numbering from right to left would place it at carbon-3, which is incorrect.

**Step 3: Assemble the IUPAC name**
Combining the substituent position with the parent chain yields **2-methylbutane**.

**Step 4: Final Result**
The systematic name is **2-methylbutane**.

cards.title: Mnemonic — Alcohols Are Cool, Acids Are Sour
body: −OH tastes of “ol” names (ethanol). −COOH are the acids. Ester = “sweet smell” from acid + alcohol minus water.

cards.title: 2.3 Derivatives — functional groups
body: **Soaps** = sodium / potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids (from fats + NaOH). They have a ionic head (loves water) and a hydrocarbon tail (loves grease) — that is why they lift dirt. **Soapless detergents** work in hard water where soap forms scum.
**Polymers** = many monomers covalently joined.

- **Addition polymerisation** — unsaturated monomers (ethene → polyethene). Double bond opens and links.
- **Condensation polymerisation** — water (or another small molecule) is kicked out. Polyesters, nylon (amide link).
Thermoplastic (PE, PVC) can be remelted. Thermoset (vulcanised rubber) cannot. Plastics pile up as waste if not reused.

cards.title: Key takeaways
body: - Addition vs condensation polymers.

cards.title: 2.3.1 Alcohols
body: “Fermentation” refers to the conversion of sugar to alcohol using yeast (a fungus).
The process of fermentation produces items such as wine, beer and yoghurt.
To make wine, grape juice is fermented to produce alcohol.
Ethanol is a diuretic (causing an increase in urination).

cards.title: 2.3.2 Carboxylic Acid
body: Carboxylic acids are organic acids that are characterized by having a carboxyl group, which has the formula —(C=O)—OH, or more commonly written as —COOH.
Carboxylic acids can have one, two, three or even more carboxyl groups.
The first two of the series are commonly called formic acid and acetic acid, respectively.
The higher monocarboxylic acids (called “fatty acids”) are also known by their common names.

cards.title: 2.3.3 Other Derivatives of Hydrocarbons
body: Other families include the aldehydes, ketones, esters and amides.
In the IUPAC system aldehydes are named after the parent hydrocarbon by replacing the last -e with -al.
In the IUPAC system, ketones are also named after the corresponding alkanes by replacing the terminal -e with -one.
The position of the ketonic functional group is indicated by a number as usual.

cards.title: 2.3.4 Soaps and Detergents
body: Fatty acids are stored in fat cells of the human body as triglycerides.
When energy is abundant, fat cells store the excess energy in the fatty acids of triglycerides.
When energy is scarce, the cells break down the triglycerides, forming free fatty acids and glycerol.
In the body this break down is brought about by enzymes.

cards.title: 2.3.5 Organic Polymers
body: As its name suggests, a macromolecule is a large molecule that forms when lots of smaller molecules are joined together.
To put it more simply, a monomer is like a building block.
When lots of similar monomers are joined together by covalent bonds, they form a polymer.
The key feature that makes a polymer different from other macromolecules is the repetition of identical or similar monomers in the polymer chain.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: How many unique structural (skeletal) isomers exist for the alkane pentane ($$\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$$)?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Draw the possible carbon skeletons for $$\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$$**
- Isomer 1: Straight chain of 5 carbons:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 \text{ (n-pentane)}$$
- Isomer 2: Branched chain of 4 carbons with 1 methyl branch:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 \text{ (2-methylbutane)}$$
- Isomer 3: Highly branched chain of 3 carbons with 2 methyl branches on the middle carbon:
$$\text{C(CH}_3)_4 \text{ (2,2-dimethylpropane)}$$

**Step 2: Confirm uniqueness**
Any other structure drawn will be a duplicate of one of these three isomers upon applying IUPAC naming rules.

**Step 3: Final Result**
There are exactly **$$3$$** unique structural isomers.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the stoichiometric coefficient of oxygen ($$\text{O}_2$$) in the balanced chemical equation for the complete combustion of one mole of liquid butane ($$\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$$)?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Write the unbalanced combustion reaction equation**
$$\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{(l)} + x\text{O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow y\text{CO}_2\text{(g)} + z\text{H}_2\text{O(g)}$$

**Step 2: Balance Carbon and Hydrogen atoms**
- For $$4$$ Carbon atoms on the left, we need $$y = 4$$:
$$\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10} + x\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 4\text{CO}_2 + z\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
- For $$10$$ Hydrogen atoms on the left, we need $$z = 5$$ (since $$5 \times 2 = 10$$):
$$\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10} + x\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 4\text{CO}_2 + 5\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Step 3: Balance Oxygen atoms to find $$x$$**
The right side has $$(4 \times 2) + 5 = 13$$ oxygen atoms. Therefore, the left side must have $$13$$ oxygen atoms:
$$2x = 13 \implies x = 6.5 \text{ (or } \frac{13}{2} \text{)}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The stoichiometric coefficient per mole of butane is **$$6.5$$**.

tips.text: Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with organic molecules.
An organic molecule is one that contains carbon.
Plants use sunlight to convert carbon dioxide in the air into organic compounds through the process of photosynthesis.
Animals and other organisms then feed on plants to obtain their own organic compounds.
Fossil fuels are another important source of carbon.

The carbon atom has four valence electrons, so it can bond with many other atoms, often resulting in long chain structures. It also forms mostly covalent bonds with the atoms that it bonds to, meaning that most organic molecules are non-polar.
One important group of organic compounds is the hydrocarbons. These molecules contain carbon and hydrogen atoms only, which can be arranged in simple or complex chains and rings.
Almost all organic compounds are considered as derivatives of hydrocarbons.

Chemical Bonding and Formulas of Hydrocarbons A carbon atom is tetravalent or always forms four bonds. These four bonds could be such that the carbon atom is connected to four other atoms (where the four atoms may be carbon or hydrogen).

On the other hand, hydrogen is monovalent, always forming one bond with carbon. However, carbon atoms can form single, double or triple bonds with each other. They can also form open chains (straight or branched) or closed chains.
Organic vs inorganic: Organic: covalent, often low m.p., burn to CO₂ + H₂O, may show isomerism. Inorganic: often ionic, high m.p., no typical combustion to CO₂.
Classification: Open chain (aliphatic) vs cyclic. Saturated (only single C–C) vs unsaturated (double / triple). Aromatic = contains a benzene ring.
Exam tip: Black bottom of a cooking pot = incomplete combustion (soot) — textbook review item.
